Problem tackled — simple: Students get stuck and don't know their next coding step.
What they do: Uses past student solution paths to find a useful next edit.
What we learn / takeaway: Past student behaviour can be used to automatically generate next-step hints.
Input / Context: Current student state + historical student traces
Hint generation: Data-driven; recommends an edit that moves toward a correct state.
Critic / Validation: No LLM critic. Quality comes from the underlying transition model.
When is hint given?: Mainly when student requests/needs a hint.
Metrics / Evaluation: Student progress, completion/dropout and efficiency were studied in later work.
What they don't do: Needs enough historical data for the student's state; doesn't generate rich natural-language explanations.
What our project has: LLM-generated natural-language hints + progressive hints + user progress tracking.

Problem tackled — simple: Hint Factory struggles because programming has huge and sparse state spaces.
What they do: Looks at similar previous student states and creates a continuous representation to predict a useful next state.
What we learn / takeaway: Exact previous code isn't necessary; similar states can be used.
Input / Context: Current code + similar historical student states
When is hint given?: Hint generation based on current state
Metrics / Evaluation: Prediction accuracy against capable students; reproduction of tutor hints.
What they don't do: Still fundamentally relies on historical student data and code-state similarity; doesn't produce flexible explanations.
What our project has: We can use an LLM, so we aren't restricted to finding a previously seen/similar code state.

Paper: Comparative Study between Automatic Hint Generation Approaches in Intelligent Programming Tutors (2021/2022)
Problem tackled — simple: Traditional programming tutors are difficult to build because the number of possible programs is huge.
What they do: Reviews and compares data-driven and program-repair approaches such as Hint Factory, CTD, AST-based approaches, etc.
What we learn / takeaway: Traditional systems are good at suggesting code edits/next steps, but richer tutoring explanations are difficult.
Metrics / Evaluation: Compares strengths/weaknesses of different approaches rather than one common metric.
What they don't do: Does not provide an LLM-based natural-language tutoring loop.
What our project has: LLM can generate flexible explanations instead of only suggesting code edits.

Problem tackled — simple: A student may be struggling, but the system shouldn't blindly interrupt them with hints.
What they do: Tracks whether the student is progressing or struggling; if struggling, it offers a hint but lets the student choose whether to open it.
What we learn / takeaway: When you give a hint matters. Also, students should retain control.
When is hint given?: Adaptive: checks progress periodically and offers hint when struggling.
Metrics / Evaluation: Programming performance, learning, perceptions; also found reduced unproductive help-seeking.
What they don't do: Block-based environment; relies on structured solution data; doesn't use an LLM to generate flexible hints.
What our project has: Text-based coding + LLM hints + attempts/failures + automatic trigger + progressive hints.

Problem tackled — simple: LLMs can generate programming hints, but the quality isn't always reliable enough.
What they do: GPT-4 generates the hint; GPT-3.5 acts as a simulated student to validate it. They also give GPT-4 failing tests/fixes as symbolic information.
What we learn / takeaway: A generated hint should be checked before being shown to the student. This is the strongest paper for our critic-agent idea.
Input / Context: Problem + buggy code + failing tests + fixed program
Critic / Validation: GPT-3.5 simulated student validates the hint.
When is hint given?: Generates feedback for buggy programs; focus is on feedback quality rather than adaptive timing.
Metrics / Evaluation: Precision, coverage, correctness, informativeness, concealment, comprehensibility; ~95% precision with >70% coverage.
What they don't do: Doesn't focus on long-term learner history, productive struggle, or deciding whether the student needs a hint at all.
What our project has: We also track attempts/progress and can make the intervention decision; we can use a critic to evaluate generated hints.

Paper: Exploring How Multiple Levels of GPT-Generated Programming Hints Support or Disappoint Novices (2024)
Problem tackled — simple: One generic LLM hint may not be enough; students may need different levels of help.
What they do: LLM Hint Factory provides 4 levels: orientation → instrumental → worked example → bottom-out.
What we learn / takeaway: Hint granularity matters. High-level hints can be too vague; more concrete hints can help with syntax/next-step issues.
When is hint given?: Student requests a hint and chooses how specific to become.
Metrics / Evaluation: Think-aloud study, hint requests, pre/post tests, successful actions, student perceptions.
What they don't do: Does not decide automatically whether the student is productively struggling; students themselves request/select the level.
What our project has: We have progressive hints + automatic triggering + user-progress information.

Paper: Howzat? Expert Judgement of Human and AI Hints (2024/2025)
Problem tackled — simple: How do we know whether an LLM-generated programming hint is actually a good hint?
What they do: Generates many hints using different LLMs/prompts and has experienced educators compare/rank them.
What we learn / takeaway: Model + prompt matter a lot. GPT-4 performed best in their study; hint length and reading level were important.
Input / Context: Student code snapshots from real programming sessions
Critic / Validation: Human expert evaluation, not an automated critic
When is hint given?: They manually selected snapshots where students appeared stuck.
Metrics / Evaluation: Comparative judgement; correctness, length, reading level, sentiment, feedback type; 80–160 words and lower reading level rated better.
What they don't do: Does not study students directly receiving hints; timing is manually selected; one-shot next-step hints.
What our project has: Our system can use ongoing student interaction rather than a single snapshot, and can eventually combine quality evaluation with intervention decisions.

Problem tackled — simple: There wasn't a unified framework for generating and evaluating hints.
What they do: Builds a framework/library for generating and evaluating hints.
What we learn / takeaway: Hint quality should be evaluated systematically, not just assumed because an LLM generated it.
Metrics / Evaluation: Relevance, readability, convergence, familiarity, answer leakage + multiple evaluation methods.
What they don't do: Mainly QA/question-based; doesn't model a student's coding history, progress or productive struggle.
What our project has: Can inspire/adapt critic metrics, but is not central to our project.

Paper: Generating Data-driven Hints for Open-ended Programming (Price, Dong & Barnes)
Problem tackled — simple: Traditional hint systems struggle with open-ended programming, where students can take many different solution paths.
What they do: Introduces CTD (Contextual Tree Decomposition), an extension of Hint Factory. It breaks the student's AST into smaller parts and learns useful edits from previous students.
What we learn / takeaway: Historical student behaviour can generate useful next-step hints even when exact student programs rarely overlap.
Input / Context: Student code snapshots + historical student traces. Tested on 51 students / 8,666 snapshots for one open-ended assignment.
Hint generation: Data-driven; uses contextual interaction networks to recommend small code changes.
Critic / Validation: No LLM critic. They evaluate generated hints against student behaviour and objectives.
When is hint given?: Primarily hint generation when a hint is requested; not focused on adaptive intervention.
Metrics / Evaluation: Objective completion, whether hints undo objectives, and whether hints move students closer to their eventual solution using Robust Tree Edit Distance. CTD-All got 35.47% of hints closer to final solution vs 60.97% for students' actual next actions.
What they don't do: Only evaluated one assignment; no real student learning study yet. Also cannot guarantee correctness because it doesn't use test cases.
What our project has: LLM-based natural-language hints rather than relying on historical code states; progressive hints, progress tracking and hint evaluation.

Paper: Next-Step Hint Generation for Introductory Programming Using Large Language Models (Roest, Keuning & Jeuring, 2023/2024)
Problem tackled — simple: Can LLMs give students useful next-step programming hints without simply giving them the solution?
What they do: Experiments with prompts and builds StAP-tutor, an LLM-based Python tutoring interface.
What we learn / takeaway: LLMs can give personalised, concise hints without requiring huge historical datasets — but they can still be misleading and too vague at later stages.
Input / Context: Problem description + student's current code; dataset of novice Python code snapshots.
Hint generation: GPT-3.5; prompt engineering to generate one next step.
Critic / Validation: No separate critic. Two human experts evaluate hints.
When is hint given?: Student asks for a hint. Automatic timing was explicitly outside their scope.
Metrics / Evaluation: Student ratings + expert evaluation: personalised, appropriate, specific, misleading information, feedback type, level of detail, tone, length. Students generally liked the hints, but all wanted more support as problems became complex.
What they don't do: Only 3 students; no learning-gain measurement. Doesn't automatically decide when to intervene.
What our project has: We can combine LLM hint generation with student-progress/attempt information and automatic triggering. We also have the opportunity for a critic/validation stage.

Paper: Navigating the Landscape of Hint Generation Research: From the Past to the Future (Jangra et al., 2024)
Problem tackled — simple: The research field is fragmented: many different approaches exist, but there isn't one clear framework for what a good hint-generation system should be.
What they do: Survey paper covering educational theory, traditional programming hint systems, LLM approaches, evaluation and future directions.
What we learn / takeaway: A good hint isn't just "correct." It should consider context, learner needs, scaffolding, clarity, prior knowledge, timing and learning objectives.
Input / Context: Literature across education, programming, NLP and ITS.
Hint generation: Reviews many generation approaches rather than building one.
Critic / Validation: Discusses the need for better evaluation rather than providing our type of critic.
When is hint given?: Highlights just-in-time interventions and personalization as important.
Metrics / Evaluation: Says current evaluation often focuses too much on whether the learner reaches the answer; better evaluation should also consider learner ownership, long-term capability, motivation and enjoyment.
What they don't do: It's a survey/roadmap, not an implemented coding tutor.
What our project has: This is useful for our research justification: our project can be framed around combining hint generation, learner context, validation and intervention rather than treating hint generation as just text generation.

Problem tackled — simple: Huge number of possible programming states makes it difficult to give a useful next step.
What they do: Uses the student's current program state and previous student states to find a path toward a correct solution.
What we learn / takeaway: Don't immediately reveal the solution; guide the learner through smaller next steps.
Input / Context: Current code, previous student states, test results, goal state
When is hint given?: Hint requested/generated for the current state
Metrics / Evaluation: Program-state/path evaluation; compares generated paths with student behaviour.
What they don't do: No LLM; doesn't dynamically decide intervention based on ongoing progress; limited authentic student evaluation.
What our project has: LLM-generated natural-language hints + progress tracking + automatic triggering + progressive assistance.

Paper: Adaptive Learning Systems in Programming Education
Problem tackled — simple: Different learners need different kinds of feedback; generic feedback may not be appropriate.
What they do: Combines program analysis, learner modelling, GPT-4 and RAG to provide personalised formative feedback.
What we learn / takeaway: Feedback should consider the learner's state, not just their code. Also shows the importance of avoiding unnecessary interruption.
Input / Context: Student code, program analysis, learner model, task information
Hint generation: GPT-4 generates personalised feedback using learner/task context.
When is hint given?: Mainly student-controlled; automatic support can occur when obvious struggle is detected.
Metrics / Evaluation: Feedback quality and system behaviour; focuses on personalised formative feedback.
What they don't do: Doesn't focus on our full progress → intervention → assistance-level policy.
What our project has: Uses attempts/progress to control intervention and progressive LLM assistance.

Problem tackled — simple: LLM programming feedback can be expensive, slow and raise privacy concerns when generated remotely.
What they do: Runs smaller LLMs in the browser using fine-tuning/quantisation.
What we learn / takeaway: Quality isn't the only concern; cost, latency and privacy matter too.
Metrics / Evaluation: Hint quality, inference time, cost and privacy/deployment considerations.
What they don't do: Doesn't focus on when to intervene or how much help a learner needs.
What our project has: Our main focus is the tutoring policy; we can use these deployment concerns for feasibility.

Problem tackled — simple: Generated hints can vary in quality, so we need a way to identify the helpful ones.
What they do: Builds a human-annotated hint dataset and develops HintRank to rank/evaluate hints.
What we learn / takeaway: Hint generation and hint evaluation are separate problems; a generated hint shouldn't automatically be trusted.
Hint generation: Hint generation/ranking in a QA setting.
When is hint given?: Not focused on adaptive programming intervention.
Metrics / Evaluation: Human helpfulness rankings; relevance/convergence and other hint-quality characteristics.
What they don't do: QA rather than programming; doesn't model student code, attempts, progress or intervention timing.
What our project has: LLM generates → critic evaluates → appropriate hint is delivered in a programming setting.
